text: Arrange in a logical order. (1) It was returned within a week. (2) She borrowed a book from the library. (3) The librarian renewed it for her. (4) She had not finished reading it.
explanation: The sequence is: she borrows (2), she has not finished (4), so the librarian renews it (3), and it is returned a week later (1). Order 2-4-3-1. Putting the return before the renewal leaves the renewal with nothing to explain it.

text: Arrange in a logical order. (1) The results were announced on Friday. (2) Three hundred students sat the test. (3) Ninety of them cleared every section. (4) The test was held in two halls.
explanation: Set the scene first -- the number of candidates (2) and where they sat (4) -- then the announcement (1), then what it revealed (3). Order 2-4-1-3. The count of those who cleared can only come after the results are out.

text: Arrange in a logical order. (1) But it cannot see whether the student understood it. (2) A platform can see that a program passes every test. (3) That is a limit of the measurement, not a bug in the platform. (4) So the number it reports should be labelled for what it is.
explanation: The claim comes first (2), then the contrast introduced by 'But' (1), then the comment on that contrast (3), then the consequence signalled by 'So' (4). Order 2-1-3-4. 'But' and 'So' are the two signposts that fix the order.

text: Arrange in a logical order. (1) Each of them is a different kind of evidence. (2) A mock interview, a written answer and a supervised sitting all tell you something. (3) Averaging them into one figure hides which is which. (4) So a reader should be shown them separately.
explanation: The list comes first (2), then what the items have in common (1), then the problem with combining them (3), then the recommendation after 'So' (4). Order 2-1-3-4.

text: Arrange in a logical order. (1) A password is something a person knows. (2) A code from a phone is something they have. (3) The two are stopped by different means, which is the whole point. (4) Anyone who learns it becomes that person as far as the system can tell.
explanation: Define the first factor (1), state its consequence (4), introduce the second factor by contrast (2), then draw the conclusion (3). Order 1-4-2-3. Sentence 4's 'it' refers to the password, so it must follow 1 immediately.

text: Arrange in a logical order. (1) The honest answer is to publish the conditions alongside the score. (2) A score from an unsupervised sitting is not the same evidence as one from a supervised hall. (3) Treating them as interchangeable is what makes a leaderboard misleading. (4) Nobody is served by a number whose provenance is hidden.
explanation: The distinction first (2), what goes wrong when it is ignored (3), the general statement of why that matters (4), then the remedy (1). Order 2-3-4-1.

text: Arrange in a logical order. (1) A device remembered for a month turns the second factor off for a month. (2) Each convenience weakens the idea in proportion to how convenient it is. (3) A code sent by message crosses a network somebody else runs. (4) That is a reason to choose them deliberately, not a reason to refuse them all.
explanation: The general claim (2), then two examples of it (3 and 1, in the order the examples escalate), then the qualification (4). Order 2-3-1-4. Sentence 4's 'them' needs the examples to have been given first.

text: Arrange in a logical order. (1) She revised the three weakest topics first. (2) Her mock test report listed six topics below the cutoff. (3) The next report showed two of them above it. (4) Three weeks remained before the campus drive.
explanation: The report comes first (2), then the constraint it had to be acted on within (4), then the action (1), then the outcome (3). Order 2-4-1-3.

text: Fill the blank: 'The department ___ the results only after two staff members have signed them off.'
options: releases|release|released|releasing
explanation: The subject 'department' is singular and the sentence states a standing practice, so the simple present 'releases' fits. 'Release' breaks agreement, the past tense contradicts the general statement, and 'releasing' is not a finite verb.

text: Fill the blank: 'A single number should not be the whole account of a student, ___ it is the easiest thing to publish.'
options: even though|because|so that|unless
explanation: The two halves pull against each other -- it should not be the whole account, and yet it is easy to publish -- so a concessive link is needed: 'even though'. 'Because' would make the ease a reason for the recommendation, which reverses the sense.

explanation: The second half is the consequence of the first, which 'so' signals. The other three set up a contrast or a condition, and there is none here.

explanation: Keeping both together means a single theft gets both, which brings back the one-secret situation: 'restores'. 'Prevents' reverses the meaning and the other two are too weak for what actually happens.

options: cannot|can|does|will

text: According to the passage, which of these can a coding platform observe directly?
options: How long a program took to run|Whether the student recognised the problem|Whether the solution was reasoned out|Whether the student could explain it a week later
explanation: The first paragraph lists what the platform sees: whether a program compiles, whether it produces the expected output, and how long a program took to run. The other three are named in the same paragraph as things it cannot see.
passage:
A coding platform measures what it can see. It sees whether a program compiles, whether it produces the expected output on each test, and how long it took to run. From those it can say, with some confidence, that a student has solved a particular problem within a particular limit. What it cannot see is almost everything a recruiter actually wants to know: whether the student understood the problem or recognised it, whether the solution was reasoned out or recalled, and whether the same student could explain the approach to a colleague the following week.

This gap is not a defect to be engineered away. It is a property of the measurement. A platform that tried to close it by inference -- by scoring confidence from typing speed, or inferring understanding from the number of attempts -- would be replacing a narrow measurement it can defend with a broad one it cannot. The honest response is to say what the number means and to put the things it does not cover somewhere a person can look: a mock interview with a mentor who asks why, a written answer that has to be read, a supervised sitting whose conditions are recorded.

The practical consequence is that a single number should never be the whole account of a student. A platform can hold several kinds of evidence and label each with how it was gathered, so that a reader can weigh them. What it should not do is average them into one figure and present that figure as though it were measured rather than assembled.
passageTitle: What a practice platform can and cannot measure

text: According to the passage, why is a leaked password a complete failure rather than a partial one?
options: Anyone who knows it becomes that person for every purpose the system can test|Passwords are usually too short to resist guessing|Systems rarely notice that a password has leaked|Most people reuse the same password everywhere
explanation: The first paragraph says exactly this: anyone who comes to know it has, for every purpose a system can test, become that person. Length, detection and reuse are real problems but are not the reason the passage gives.
passage:
A password is something a person knows. Anyone who comes to know it has, for every purpose a system can test, become that person. This is why a leaked password is not a partial failure: it is a complete one, and the system that accepted it behaved correctly throughout.

A second factor is valuable precisely because it is not another thing to know. A code from an application on a phone is something the person has, and it changes every thirty seconds, so knowing it is worth almost nothing a minute later. An attacker who has learned a password by reading a note, watching a keyboard or buying a list is stopped not because the second factor is harder to guess but because it is a different KIND of thing, and the way they obtained the first does not obtain the second.

It follows that the common conveniences weaken the idea in proportion to how convenient they are. A code sent by message travels over a network somebody else operates. A device remembered for thirty days turns the second factor off for thirty days. A recovery code written in the same notebook as the password restores exactly the situation the second factor was adopted to prevent. None of these is useless, and each should be chosen deliberately rather than added because it reduces support calls.
passageTitle: Why a second factor is not a second password

None of these is useless, and each should be chosen deliberately rather than added because it reduces support calls.
